specStatements.text: Students should be able to calculate the amount of energy associated with a moving object, a stretched spring and an object raised above ground level.
The kinetic energy of a moving object can be calculated using the equation:
kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)^2
kinetic energy, Ek, in joules, J
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
speed, v, in metres per second, m/s
The amount of elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring can be calculated using the equation:
elastic potential energy = 0.5 × spring constant × (extension)^2
(assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded)
elastic potential energy, Ee, in joules, J
spring constant, k, in newtons per metre, N/m
extension, e, in metres, m
The amount of gravitational potential energy gained by an object raised above ground level can be calculated using the equation:
g.p.e. = mass × gravitational field strength × height
[E_p = m g h]
gravitational potential energy, Ep, in joules, J
mass, m, in kilograms, kg
gravitational field strength, g, in newtons per kilogram, N/kg (In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given).
height, h, in metres, m

scopeNotes.statement: (assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded)
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every elastic potential energy calculation in this section states, or makes clear, that the spring is still within its limit of proportionality, so the equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2 is always applied inside its stated range. No item asks for the energy stored in a spring stretched beyond that limit, and no replacement equation is offered for that case; the one item that goes near the boundary asks only that students recognise the equation can no longer be used.

scopeNotes.statement: In any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength (g) will be given.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every gravitational potential energy calculation states the value of g inside the question itself, so no item depends on recalling a value. One item makes the provision explicit by asking students where the value of g comes from.

concepts.definition: The energy stored in an object because it is moving. It is calculated from kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2, that is E_k = 1/2 m v^2, and it is zero when the object is at rest.

In E_k = 1/2 m v^2 the speed alone is squared, not the mass and not the product of the two. Doubling the speed of an object multiplies its kinetic energy by four, while doubling its mass only doubles the kinetic energy.

concepts.term: Units in the kinetic energy equation
concepts.definition: Kinetic energy Ek is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; speed v is in metres per second, m/s. A mass in grams or a speed in km/h must be converted first, or the answer will not be in joules.

The unit of every energy store in this section: kinetic, elastic potential and gravitational potential energy are all measured in joules. The newton is a unit of force and the watt is a unit of power, so neither can be the unit of an energy calculation.

The energy stored in a spring, or other elastic object, because it has been stretched or compressed. For a spring it is calculated from elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2, that is E_e = 1/2 k e^2.
A measure of how stiff a spring is: the force needed for each metre of extension. It is measured in newtons per metre, N/m, so a spring of large k needs a large force to stretch it a given amount.

The increase in the length of the spring, measured in metres, m. It is the stretched length minus the original unstretched length, not the stretched length itself, and it must be converted from centimetres or millimetres before it is squared.

The point beyond which extension is no longer proportional to the force applied. The equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2 is used only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded; past that point it no longer gives the energy stored.

The energy stored in an object because of its position in a gravitational field. The amount gained when an object is raised is calculated from g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height, that is E_p = m g h.
The force acting on each kilogram of mass, measured in newtons per kilogram, N/kg. Its value is always supplied in the question in this specification, so it never has to be recalled.

The vertical distance the object is raised above ground level, measured in metres, m. When an object is moved along a slope or a ramp, it is the vertical rise that is used as h, not the longer distance travelled along the surface.
In E_p = m g h the gravitational potential energy Ep is in joules, J; mass m is in kilograms, kg; gravitational field strength g is in newtons per kilogram, N/kg; and height h is in metres, m.

concepts.term: Units in the elastic potential energy equation
concepts.definition: In E_e = 1/2 k e^2 the elastic potential energy Ee is in joules, J; the spring constant k is in newtons per metre, N/m; and the extension e is in metres, m.

Mass is the quantity of matter in an object, measured in kilograms, kg, and it is m in E_k = 1/2 m v^2 and E_p = m g h. No mass appears in E_e = 1/2 k e^2. Weight is a force in newtons and is never substituted for the mass.

Use E_k = 1/2 m v^2 when an object is moving, E_e = 1/2 k e^2 when a spring has been stretched, and E_p = m g h when an object has been raised. Only the kinetic and elastic equations contain a factor of 0.5.

misconceptions.question: A trolley of mass 2 kg moves at 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
misconceptions.misconception: You work out 0.5 x 2 x 5 = 5 J, using the speed but never squaring it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is remembered as the spoken phrase 'half m v', and the small index is lost when it is written out from memory under time pressure.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2. Square the speed first and write the squared value down (5^2 = 25) before multiplying by the mass and by 0.5.

misconceptions.question: A cyclist doubles her speed. What happens to her kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes four times as large, because the speed is squared.
misconceptions.misconception: You say the kinetic energy doubles as well, because the speed has doubled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Most GCSE relationships met before this point are directly proportional, so doubling one quantity is expected to double the other.
misconceptions.correction: Only speed is squared in E_k = 1/2 m v^2, so a factor of 2 on the speed becomes a factor of 2^2 = 4 on the energy. Test it with numbers: 0.5 x 60 x 4^2 = 480 J, but 0.5 x 60 x 8^2 = 1920 J.

misconceptions.question: A ball of mass 500 g moves at 6 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
misconceptions.misconception: You substitute 500 straight into the equation and obtain 9000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The number in the question is the one that feels 'given', and the unit written next to it is read over rather than checked.
misconceptions.correction: The equation requires the mass in kilograms. Divide a mass in grams by 1000 before substituting: 500 g = 0.5 kg.

misconceptions.question: A car travels at 72 km/h. What speed is used in E_k = 1/2 m v^2?
misconceptions.correct: The speed must first be converted to metres per second, giving 20 m/s.
misconceptions.misconception: You substitute 72 as the speed, or convert it into some other unit such as kilometres per minute.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Everyday speeds are quoted in km/h or mph, so those units feel like the natural ones for a speed.
misconceptions.correction: In this equation the speed must be in metres per second, m/s, because that is the only speed unit that gives an energy in joules.

misconceptions.question: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m. Find the energy stored.
misconceptions.misconception: You leave out the factor of 0.5 and work out 200 x 0.1^2 = 2 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 0.5 looks like a small tidying-up number rather than part of the physics, so it is dropped when the equation is rewritten quickly.
misconceptions.correction: Both E_k = 1/2 m v^2 and E_e = 1/2 k e^2 begin with a factor of 0.5, and leaving it out doubles every answer.

misconceptions.question: A ball has a mass of 0.25 kg. What is substituted for m?
misconceptions.misconception: You convert the mass into a weight in newtons first, or you describe the mass in grams as a weight.
misconceptions.whyItArises: In everyday speech 'weight' is used for what a balance measures, so mass and weight are treated as the same quantity with a choice of units.
misconceptions.correction: Mass is measured in kilograms and is what m stands for in E_k = 1/2 m v^2 and E_p = m g h; the elastic potential energy equation contains no mass. Weight is a force in newtons and is never substituted for m.

misconceptions.question: A trolley of mass 2 kg moves at 5 m/s. Find its kinetic energy.
misconceptions.misconception: You work out 0.5 x 5^2 = 12.5 J, leaving the mass out altogether.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The squaring of the speed takes all the attention, and the mass is the quantity most easily forgotten once the square has been dealt with.
misconceptions.correction: Three numbers are multiplied together in E_k = 1/2 m v^2: 0.5, the mass and the squared speed. Check that all three appear in your working.

misconceptions.question: A spring of natural length 0.20 m is stretched to 0.26 m. What is the extension?
misconceptions.misconception: You use 0.26 m, the whole stretched length, or 0.20 m, the length before stretching.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The stretched length is the number the ruler shows at the end of the experiment, so it is read as 'the length of the spring' without subtracting.
misconceptions.correction: The extension is the increase in length: stretched length minus original length. It is zero for an unstretched spring, which the total length never is.

misconceptions.question: A spring of spring constant 400 N/m has an extension of 5 cm. Find the energy stored.
misconceptions.misconception: You substitute 5 for the extension and obtain 5000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Extensions are measured with a centimetre ruler, so the centimetre reading is the number in front of the student when the equation is written.
misconceptions.correction: The extension must be in metres before it is squared. Divide a centimetre value by 100: 5 cm = 0.05 m. Squaring magnifies the error, so an unconverted value is out by a factor of 10 000.

misconceptions.question: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m is stretched by 0.1 m. Find the energy stored.
misconceptions.misconception: You work out 0.5 x 200 x 0.1 = 10 J, never squaring the extension.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The extension is a small decimal, and squaring a decimal feels wrong because the answer gets smaller, so the step is skipped.
misconceptions.correction: The equation is elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2. Square the extension first: 0.1^2 = 0.01.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of the spring constant k?
misconceptions.misconception: You give newtons per kilogram, N/kg, or newton metres, N m.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Several similar-looking compound units appear in this part of the course, and they are stored as a list of symbols rather than attached to their quantities.
misconceptions.correction: The spring constant is the force needed per metre of extension, so it is newtons per metre, N/m. N/kg belongs to gravitational field strength, and N m is a unit of energy.

misconceptions.question: A spring is stretched past its limit of proportionality. Can E_e = 1/2 k e^2 still be used?
misconceptions.correct: No. The equation applies only while the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded.
misconceptions.misconception: You carry on using the equation with the same spring constant, or assume the spring constant simply takes a new fixed value.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is learned as a formula that works for springs, and the bracketed condition in the specification is read as a side note rather than a restriction.
misconceptions.correction: The specification states the equation assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded. Beyond that limit, extension is no longer proportional to force and the equation no longer gives the energy stored.

misconceptions.question: A book of mass 0.8 kg is lifted 1.5 m. g = 10 N/kg. Find the g.p.e. gained.
misconceptions.misconception: You work out 0.8 x 1.5 = 1.2 J, leaving the gravitational field strength out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass and height are the two quantities that describe the object and the lift, so g feels like a constant that is quoted rather than used.
misconceptions.correction: Three quantities are multiplied in E_p = m g h. The value of g is given in the question precisely because it must be substituted.

misconceptions.question: A book of mass 0.8 kg is lifted 1.5 m. g = 10 N/kg. Find the g.p.e. gained.
misconceptions.misconception: You work out 0.5 x 0.8 x 10 x 1.5 = 6 J, putting a factor of 0.5 into the equation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The other two energy equations in this section both start with 0.5, so the half is carried across as though every energy equation had one.
misconceptions.correction: g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height. There is no factor of 0.5: the half appears only where a quantity is squared.

misconceptions.question: A box is pushed 5.0 m along a ramp and ends 2.0 m above the ground. What is h?
misconceptions.correct: h = 2.0 m, the vertical height gained.
misconceptions.misconception: You use one of the other distances in the problem instead of the vertical height h - the distance travelled along the ramp, or a sum or difference of the given distances - not realising h must be the vertical rise above the starting level.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The 5.0 m is the distance the box actually travelled, so it feels like the quantity that describes the movement.
misconceptions.correction: In E_p = m g h, h is the vertical height above the starting level. The path taken does not change the gravitational potential energy gained.

misconceptions.question: Where does the value of g come from in a g.p.e. calculation?
misconceptions.correct: It is given in the question; the specification states that the value of g will be supplied.
misconceptions.misconception: You believe the value must be memorised, and worry about whether to use 9.8 or 10.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Two different values appear in textbooks and past papers, so students assume recall is being tested.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says that in any calculation the value of the gravitational field strength will be given. Read the value from the question and use it as printed.

misconceptions.question: What unit does a kinetic or elastic potential energy calculation give?
misconceptions.misconception: You give newtons, N, or watts, W.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Newtons and watts are the units met alongside energy in mechanics, and unit symbols are memorised as a set rather than paired with their quantities.
misconceptions.correction: Every energy store in this section is measured in joules, J. The newton is a unit of force and the watt is a unit of power.

misconceptions.question: A van doubles its speed while its mass stays the same. What happens to its kinetic energy?
misconceptions.correct: It becomes four times as large.
misconceptions.misconception: You say it is unchanged, because the mass of the van has not changed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Mass is the quantity that feels permanent and object-like, so it is treated as the thing that fixes the energy an object has.
misconceptions.correction: Kinetic energy depends on both mass and speed, and on the square of the speed. A stationary van has no kinetic energy at all, whatever its mass.

misconceptions.question: A book of mass 800 g is lifted 1.5 m. g = 10 N/kg. Find the g.p.e. gained.
misconceptions.misconception: You substitute 800 for the mass and obtain 12 000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The conversion is an extra step that is easily skipped when the arithmetic itself looks straightforward.
misconceptions.correction: The mass in E_p = m g h must be in kilograms. Convert first: 800 g = 0.8 kg.

misconceptions.question: Which quantity is squared in the kinetic energy equation?
misconceptions.correct: The speed, giving E_k = 1/2 m v^2.
misconceptions.misconception: You square the mass instead, using 0.5 x (mass)^2 x speed.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is recalled as 'a half, a mass, a speed and a square', and the square is attached to whichever symbol is written first.
misconceptions.correction: Only the speed is squared. Writing the equation in words as kinetic energy = 0.5 x mass x (speed)^2 keeps the bracket around the right quantity.

misconceptions.question: In E_e = 1/2 k e^2, what does e stand for?
misconceptions.correct: The extension of the spring, in metres.
misconceptions.misconception: You read e as the energy stored, or as the mathematical constant e.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The subscript in Ee and the symbol e look alike, so the two are read as the same thing.
misconceptions.correction: Ee is the elastic potential energy and e is the extension. The equation therefore has energy on one side and extension, squared, on the other.

misconceptions.question: In E_e = 1/2 k e^2, what does e stand for?
misconceptions.correct: The extension of the spring, in metres.
misconceptions.misconception: You read e as the effort, or force, applied to the spring.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Force is what causes the stretch, so it is the quantity students expect an equation about stretching to contain.
misconceptions.correction: The force does not appear in this equation. Its effect is already contained in the extension e and the spring constant k.

misconceptions.question: Which quantities are needed to find the kinetic energy of a moving object?
misconceptions.misconception: You look for the force applied to it or the distance it has travelled.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Work done is calculated from force and distance, and that equation is met close to this one, so its quantities are borrowed.
misconceptions.correction: Kinetic energy is worked out from mass and speed alone. Force and distance give the work done, which is a different calculation.

misconceptions.question: Which quantities are needed to find the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring?
misconceptions.correct: The spring constant and the extension.
misconceptions.misconception: You look for the mass of the spring, or for the force stretching it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The other two energy equations in this section both contain a mass, so a mass is expected here too.
misconceptions.correction: E_e = 1/2 k e^2 contains no mass and no force: only the spring constant, in N/m, and the extension, in m.

misconceptions.question: What is the unit of gravitational field strength g?
misconceptions.misconception: You give newtons, N, because you think g is the force of gravity itself.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The phrase 'the pull of gravity' is used for both the field strength and the weight, so the two quantities merge.
misconceptions.correction: Gravitational field strength is the force acting on each kilogram, so it is newtons per kilogram, N/kg. The force itself, the weight, is in newtons.

misconceptions.question: A spring of spring constant 200 N/m has an extension of 0.1 m. Find the energy stored.
misconceptions.misconception: You square the spring constant instead of the extension, working out 0.5 x 200^2 x 0.1 = 2000 J.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The extension is a small decimal that gets smaller when squared, which feels wrong, so the square is moved onto the larger, more equation-looking number.
misconceptions.correction: In E_e = 1/2 k e^2 the index belongs to the extension only. Writing the equation in words as elastic potential energy = 0.5 x spring constant x (extension)^2 keeps the bracket in the right place.

mcqs.stem: A ball of mass 500 g is moving at a speed of 6 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.text: 9 J

options.rationale: Obtained from 0.5 x 500 x 36, with the mass left in grams.
Obtained from 0.5 x 0.5 x 6, with the speed never squared.
Obtained from 0.5 x 36, with the factor of 0.5 applied to nothing and the mass dropped, or from 0.5 kg x 36 with no half.

mcqs.stem: A toy car of mass 0.8 kg is moving at a speed of 5 m/s. What is its kinetic energy?

options.text: 2 J
options.rationale: Obtained from 0.5 x 0.8 x 5: the speed has been used but not squared.
Obtained from 0.5 x 5^2, with the mass left out of the calculation.
Obtained from 0.5 x 0.8^2 x 5, squaring the mass instead of the speed.

mcqs.stem: A van doubles its speed. Its mass does not change. What happens to its kinetic energy?

options.text: it grows in the same ratio as the speed
options.rationale: Treats kinetic energy as proportional to speed (m02); it depends on speed squared, so four times.

options.text: it becomes four times as large as before
options.rationale: Speed is squared in E_k = 1/2 m v^2, so a factor of 2 on the speed gives a factor of 2^2 = 4 on the energy.

options.text: it becomes twice as large as before
options.rationale: Chosen by treating kinetic energy as directly proportional to speed.

options.text: it stays the same size as before
options.rationale: Chosen by students who think the mass alone fixes an object's kinetic energy.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is the equation E_k = 1/2 m v^2 written out in words?

options.text: kinetic energy = 0.5 × (mass)^2 × (speed)
options.rationale: The square has been attached to the mass rather than to the speed.

options.text: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × speed
options.rationale: The squaring of the speed has been dropped.

options.text: kinetic energy = mass × (speed)^2
options.rationale: The factor of 0.5 has been dropped.

options.text: kinetic energy = 0.5 × mass × (speed)^2
options.rationale: This is the equation as the specification states it: the speed, and only the speed, is squared.

mcqs.stem: A kinetic energy calculation uses a mass in kilograms and a speed in metres per second. The answer is in which unit?

options.text: newtons, N
options.rationale: The newton is the unit of force, not of energy.

options.text: watts, W
options.rationale: The watt is the unit of power: energy transferred each second, not the energy itself.

options.text: joules, J
options.rationale: Kinetic energy, like every energy store in this section, is measured in joules, J.

options.text: kg m/s
options.rationale: These are the units of mass and speed multiplied together, which is momentum rather than energy.

mcqs.stem: A student puts the mass of a 250 g ball straight into E_k = 1/2 m v^2 as 250. Why is the answer wrong?

options.text: the speed should not have been squared
options.rationale: Reflects using the speed without squaring it (m01); the real fault is mass in kilograms, not grams.

options.text: the mass has to be in newtons, so m should be 2.5
options.rationale: Newtons measure weight, which is a force; m in this equation is a mass in kilograms.

options.text: the answer is right, but the unit is newtons
options.rationale: The unit is wrong here as well as the number: an energy calculation gives joules.

options.text: the mass has to be in kilograms, so m should be 0.25
options.rationale: The equation needs the mass in kilograms, and 250 g = 250/1000 = 0.25 kg.

mcqs.stem: A car's speed is given as 72 km/h. What must be done before using E_k = 1/2 m v^2?

options.text: convert the speed to metres per second
options.rationale: The equation requires the speed v in m/s, so 72 km/h must be converted to 20 m/s first.

options.text: convert the speed into kilometres per minute
options.rationale: Kilometres per minute is no more use here than km/h: the equation needs metres per second.

options.text: use 72 as the speed and convert the answer
options.rationale: Substituting 72 gives a number that cannot be converted into joules afterwards.

options.text: square 72 first and then halve the answer
options.rationale: This does the arithmetic of the equation but on an unconverted speed, and it also leaves out the mass.

mcqs.stem: Which pair of quantities is needed to calculate the kinetic energy of a moving object?

options.text: the force applied and the speed reached
options.rationale: Force and distance give the work done, which is a different calculation from kinetic energy.

options.text: the weight and the speed of the object
options.rationale: The weight is a force in newtons; m in the equation is the mass in kilograms.

options.text: the mass and the speed of the object
options.rationale: E_k = 1/2 m v^2 contains only the mass and the speed; nothing else about the object is needed.

options.text: the mass and the distance travelled
options.rationale: How far the object has travelled does not appear in the kinetic energy equation.

mcqs.stem: A spring has a spring constant of 200 N/m. It is stretched, within its limit of proportionality, so that its extension is 0.1 m. How much elastic potential energy is stored in the spring?

options.rationale: Obtained from 0.5 x 200 x 0.1, with the extension never squared.
Obtained from 0.5 x 200^2 x 0.1, squaring the spring constant instead of the extension.

options.text: 1 J

options.rationale: Obtained from 0.5 x 200 x 10^2, with the extension used as 10 cm instead of 0.1 m.

mcqs.stem: A spring with a spring constant of 400 N/m is stretched by an extension of 5 cm, staying within its limit of proportionality. How much elastic potential energy is stored?

options.text: 1 J
options.rationale: Obtained from 400 x 0.05^2, with the factor of 0.5 left out.
Obtained from 0.5 x 400 x 0.05, with the extension never squared.
Obtained from 0.5 x 400 x 5^2, with the extension left in centimetres.

mcqs.stem: The energy stored in a stretched spring is E_e = 1/2 k e^2. What do the symbols k and e stand for?

options.text: the spring constant and the energy of the spring
options.rationale: The energy is Ee, on the left of the equation; e on the right is the extension.

options.text: the spring constant and the force applied to it
options.rationale: The force does not appear in this equation; its effect is contained in k and e.

options.text: the spring constant and the stretched length
options.rationale: The extension is the increase in length, not the full stretched length.

options.text: the spring constant and the extension of the spring
options.rationale: k is the spring constant, in N/m, and e is the extension, in m.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched within its limit of proportionality. The elastic potential energy stored in it is measured in which unit?

options.text: newtons, N
options.rationale: The newton is the unit of the force stretching the spring, not of the energy stored.

options.text: joules, J
options.rationale: Elastic potential energy, like every energy store, is measured in joules, J.

options.text: watts, W
options.rationale: The watt is the unit of power, not of stored energy.

options.text: N/kg, newtons per kilogram
options.rationale: Gives N/kg from unit confusion (m11); elastic potential energy is measured in joules.

mcqs.stem: In the equation E_e = 1/2 k e^2, the spring constant k is measured in which unit?

options.text: newtons times metres, N m
options.rationale: A newton metre is a unit of energy, which is what the equation gives, not what k is measured in.

options.text: newtons per kilogram, N/kg
options.rationale: Newtons per kilogram is the unit of gravitational field strength, not of a spring constant.

options.text: newtons per centimetre, N/cm
options.rationale: The specification gives the spring constant in newtons per metre; extensions are converted to metres, not the other way round.

options.text: newtons per metre, N/m
options.rationale: The spring constant is the force needed for each metre of extension, so it is measured in N/m.

mcqs.stem: A spring of unstretched length 0.20 m is stretched to a length of 0.26 m. Which length is the extension e used in E_e = 1/2 k e^2?

options.text: the whole stretched length, in metres
options.rationale: 0.26 m is the stretched length; the extension is how much longer the spring has become.

options.text: the increase in length, in metres
options.rationale: The extension is 0.26 - 0.20 = 0.06 m, and the equation needs it in metres.

options.text: the length before stretching, in metres
options.rationale: 0.20 m is the unstretched length, which is the value subtracted, not the extension itself.

options.text: the extra length, in centimetres
options.rationale: The increase in length is right, but 6 cm must be converted to 0.06 m before it is squared.

mcqs.stem: A spring is stretched so far that its limit of proportionality has been exceeded. What does this mean for E_e = 1/2 k e^2?

options.text: the equation still works if e is measured again
options.rationale: Re-measuring the extension does not help: past the limit the extension is no longer proportional to the force.

options.text: the spring constant doubles from that point on
options.rationale: There is no new fixed spring constant beyond the limit; the proportional relationship has broken down.

options.text: the equation can no longer be used to find the energy
options.rationale: The specification states the equation assuming the limit of proportionality has not been exceeded, so beyond that limit it does not apply.

options.text: the stored energy still rises with e squared
options.rationale: Assumes E_e = 1/2 k e^2 still applies beyond the limit (m12); the equation no longer holds.

mcqs.stem: Which two quantities must be known to calculate the elastic potential energy stored in a stretched spring?

options.text: the spring constant and the extension
options.rationale: E_e = 1/2 k e^2 needs only the spring constant k, in N/m, and the extension e, in m.

options.text: the spring constant and the force used
options.rationale: The stretching force does not appear in the equation; the extension it produces does.

options.text: the mass of the spring and its extension
options.rationale: No mass appears in the elastic potential energy equation.

options.text: the spring constant and the length
options.rationale: It is the extension, not the length of the spring, that is squared in the equation.

mcqs.stem: A book of mass 800 g is lifted through a height of 1.5 m. The gravitational field strength is 10 N/kg. How much gravitational potential energy does the book gain?

options.rationale: Obtained from 800 x 10 x 1.5, with the mass left in grams.

options.text: 6 J
options.rationale: Obtained from 0.5 x 0.8 x 10 x 1.5, with a factor of 0.5 brought in from the other energy equations.
Obtained from 0.8 x 1.5, with the gravitational field strength left out.

mcqs.stem: A box is pushed 5.0 m up a ramp and ends up 2.0 m above the ground. Which value is used as h in E_p = m g h?

options.text: 5.0 m, the distance moved along the ramp surface
options.rationale: 5.0 m is the distance travelled along the slope, which is longer than the height gained.

options.text: 3.0 m, the difference in the two distances
options.rationale: Subtracting the two distances has no physical meaning here; the vertical rise is given directly.

options.text: 2.0 m, the vertical height risen above the ground
options.rationale: h is the vertical height gained, and the path taken up the ramp does not change it.

options.text: 7.0 m, the two distances added together
options.rationale: Adding the slope distance to the height counts the same lift twice.

mcqs.stem: Which of these is g.p.e. = mass x gravitational field strength x height written in symbols, with the correct unit?

options.text: E_p = 1/2 m g h, giving E_p in joules
options.rationale: There is no factor of 0.5 in the gravitational potential energy equation.

options.text: E_p = m g h, giving E_p in joules
options.rationale: This is the equation as the specification states it, and Ep is measured in joules, J.

options.text: E_p = m g h, giving E_p in watts
options.rationale: The equation is right but the unit is not: the watt is the unit of power.

options.text: E_p = m h, giving E_p in joules
options.rationale: Leaves gravitational field strength out, using only m and h (m13); correct form is m g h.

mcqs.stem: In E_p = m g h, what is g and where does its value come from?

options.text: field strength in N/kg, which must be recalled
options.rationale: The unit is right, but the value never has to be recalled: it is supplied in the question.

options.text: field strength in N, given in the exam question
options.rationale: The value is given, but the unit is wrong: newtons alone measure a force, such as weight.

options.text: the force of gravity in N, given in the question
options.rationale: g is the force on each kilogram, not the total force on the object.

options.text: field strength in N/kg, given in the question
options.rationale: Gravitational field strength is measured in newtons per kilogram, and the specification states that its value will be given.
